chapter: Joining Goodman and views on arranging
title: Form dictated by choreography in shows
summary: Form, rewrites and too many cooks.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: It's like turning black and white into color, I suppose.
Something like that. Consolation may be a better word. It takes me three months to get over one, to have some sense of what I am again.
How did it go, for example, when recently you were orchestrating for (inaudible)?
The same way. I had to work within the confines of what was there. Form is probably the worst offender. Form always takes a
(Side A of Tape 2 ended at this point. Transcript will continue with Side B.)

--Form always takes a back seat to choreography, or the need of a singer to move around, or the needs of a story. It's worse than film. In film form is given, but it's worse because in a film you can (in-audible).
So form is dictated to you, in effect, especially in a show.

Everything is dictated. There is very little of you that creeps into these things. There are too many cooks. There's always that criticism that comes from the director and choreographer and I suppose the actors as well. It forces you to change everything. If you start off with the thing, you go into rehearsal and you make a whole set and they go on the road; by the time you come back, the thing is completely rewritten, and usually with parts tacked onto it.
It doesn't make sense at all; musically it's just darn awful.

I have a friend who is a very good studio arranger in New York who was in Connecticut last summer working on the embryonic stages of the show that apparently there's a very famous little theatre in Connecticut--

I forget, but apparently a lot of the shows that make it very big on Broadway start there, and they had him come up to do the arranging and orchestrating for this when it was still in the infant stages and he was just going crazy, --
